strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated environment (PwP) that unifies diverse SWE tasks under a single computer-use (visual/keyboard/mouse) paradigm, contrasting with the prevailing hand-engineered tool-based paradigm.
PwP-Bench aggregates 15 tasks from 13 existing datasets plus 2 new ones, spanning multiple languages and modalities, providing a broader and more realistic testbed than prior narrow SWE benchmarks.
Thorough infrastructure description (Docker sandboxing, xdotool actions, checkpointing, gymnasium-style API) supports reproducibility and future extension, including RL training.

Interesting and useful empirical findings: computer-use agents can approach/surpass tool-based SOTA on some tasks (e.g., Intercode/CTF with statistical significance testing), while also revealing systematic weaknesses in visual grounding, tool usage, and error recovery, which are illustrated with clear qualitative examples (Figures 4-13).
The 'assisted' agent ablation and the rename-tool prompting experiment nicely quantify the potential headroom from better tool utilization, providing actionable insight for future agent design.

Good related-work positioning distinguishing PwP from web/OS agent benchmarks (OSWorld, VisualWebArena) and from tool-based SWE benchmarks (SWE-bench, SWE-agent), with comparison tables (Table 1, 2, 5).
weaknesses: Evaluation relies solely on PwP-Bench-Lite (300 instances, 20 per task) due to compute/budget constraints, which is a fairly small sample per task category and may not yield statistically robust comparisons across 5 models x 15 tasks x 2 settings; only one significance test (Intercode) is reported.

The 20-step iteration cap is a potentially severe constraint for complex repository-level tasks (e.g., SWE-Bench) and could unfairly penalize computer-use agents relative to tool-based baselines that may use much longer trajectories (acknowledged by authors for SWE-Bench at 55% vs their setup), undermining fair comparison claims of 'surpassing' SOTA.

Comparisons to 'previous state of the art' in Table 6 mix different model versions, tool access, and trajectory budgets, making the headline claim of computer-use agents 'approaching or exceeding' SOTA somewhat overstated and not apples-to-apples.

Only five VLMs tested, and only one (Claude) shows non-trivial performance in the pure computer-use setting; the paper's conclusions about generality of the paradigm rest heavily on a single model, weakening the generalizability claim.

The 'assisted' agent experiments used only 4 datasets (SWE-Bench, Design2Code, ChartMimic, BIRD), a small subset of the 15 tasks, limiting the strength of conclusions about the value of IDE tool access across the whole benchmark.

Reward/evaluation methodology details are relegated largely to appendix and some metrics (e.g., macro-averaging heterogeneous metrics per dataset) may obscure fine-grained comparisons; also no analysis of variance/repeated runs given the inherent stochasticity of GUI actions and timing mentioned in the POMDP definition.

No cost/efficiency analysis (e.g., number of API calls, latency, token usage) comparing computer-use vs tool-based agents, which is important for practical significance given computer-use requires many more low-level steps per task.

The claimed novelty of 'first environment for computer-use SWE agents' should be tempered given closely related generalist environments (OSWorld) already support similar screen-based interaction; the distinction is more about SWE-specificity and tooling breadth than a fundamentally new paradigm.

Limited discussion of failure case statistics (e.g., what fraction of failures are due to grounding vs planning vs tool non-use) — the analysis is largely qualitative/anecdotal (individual figures) rather than quantified systematically.

strengths: The paper proposes a conceptually interesting reframing of SWE agents as general-purpose computer-use agents operating in a full IDE (VSCode) rather than through hand-engineered tool APIs, which is a timely and relevant direction given recent interest in computer-use agents.

PwP-Bench aggregates 15 tasks across 8 languages and multiple modalities (code gen, PR resolution, UI generation, DevOps, theorem proving, CTF, etc.) into a single unified environment with a POMDP formalization, Docker-based sandboxing, checkpointing, and a gymnasium-style API, which is useful infrastructure for the community.

The analysis section provides informative qualitative failure-mode case studies (visual grounding errors, misidentified UI elements/active panels, inability to recover from errors), which could be useful for future agent design even if individually unsurprising.
The 'assisted agent' ablation, where hand-crafted API calls are added on top of the computer-use agent, is a reasonable way to quantify the current gap between potential and realized tool usage.
weaknesses: The central thesis—that computer-use agents can replace the tool-based paradigm—is undermined by the paper's own results: pure screenshot+SoM agents achieve only up to 10.2% overall, while performance only becomes competitive (46.8%) once file/bash API 'tool calls' are reintroduced, which is itself a form of the tool-based paradigm the paper argues against. This internal contradiction is not adequately addressed.

All experiments are run on PwP-Bench-Lite (300 instances, only 20 per task), which is a very small sample for a 15-task, 4-category benchmark; reported percentages (e.g., 100%, 0%, 55.7%) are likely to have wide confidence intervals and limited statistical reliability, yet are discussed as if precise.

Comparisons to 'state-of-the-art' tool-based baselines are explicitly acknowledged by the authors to be confounded by different model versions, iteration budgets (e.g., 20-step cap vs. much longer trajectories for SWE-Bench SOTA), and compute, which weakens the paper's headline claim that computer-use agents 'approach or surpass' specialized agents.

Model coverage is limited to five VLMs (GPT-4o/mini, Gemini-Flash/Pro, Claude-3.5-Sonnet) without more recent or stronger computer-use-specific models, and only Claude is 'natively trained' for UI interaction, making the central finding ('only one model performs well') somewhat tautological rather than a broad empirical finding.

13 of 15 benchmark tasks are directly repurposed from existing datasets, so the main novel contribution is largely an engineering/integration effort (wrapping these into an IDE+action space) rather than new task design; the benchmark's intellectual novelty beyond aggregation is limited.

The visual-grounding and tool-underutilization findings (poor grounding, inability to recover from errors, failure to leverage IDE tools) largely replicate findings already established in OSWorld, VisualWebArena, and related computer-use literature, offering limited new insight specific to software engineering beyond confirming the pattern holds in IDEs too.

Key reproducibility details are deferred to the appendix or missing (e.g., the code/data release link appears truncated/missing in the main text), and core evaluation details (task-specific metrics, reward functions) are only partially specified in the main paper.

No human baseline or inter-rater reliability analysis is provided to contextualize how 'solvable' the tasks are within the 20-step budget, making it hard to assess whether low scores reflect agent limitations or environment/budget constraints.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated paradigm shift from hand-engineered tool-based SWE agents to general-purpose computer-use agents operating directly in an IDE, addressing a real scalability limitation of prior tool-based approaches.

PwP-Bench is a substantial and diverse unification effort, aggregating 15 tasks across 8 programming languages and multiple modalities (code editing, PR resolution, UI generation, DevOps, data science, CTF, theorem proving), which is more comprehensive than most existing SWE benchmarks.

Solid infrastructure contribution: sandboxed Docker-based VSCode environment with checkpointing, gymnasium-style API, and multi-channel state/action interfaces, which could be broadly useful to the community.

The analysis section is thorough and insightful, clearly documenting failure modes (visual grounding errors, inability to recover from errors, inability to exploit IDE tools) with concrete qualitative examples (Figures 7-12).
The 'assisted' agent ablation nicely demonstrates the headroom available if agents better leveraged IDE tooling, providing a clear and actionable direction for future work.
Good related-work positioning and comparison tables (Tables 1, 2, 5) that clearly differentiate PwP from prior environments (OSWorld, WebArena, SWE-Bench, etc.).
weaknesses: Evaluation is conducted only on PwP-Bench-Lite (300 of 5400 instances) due to compute/budget constraints, and only 20 steps per task are allowed, which may be insufficient for realistic SWE tasks and could bias results against agents needing longer horizons; the full-scale benchmark results are never actually reported.

Absolute performance is quite low across most models/settings (e.g., <11% for pure computer-use agents, and only Claude with tool/file access surpasses 40%), which somewhat undercuts the claim that computer-use agents 'approach or surpass' tool-based SOTA — the comparison to 'previous SOTA' in Table 6 is explicitly acknowledged as apples-to-oranges (different trajectory budgets, models, tool access) and is only used for a single model on select datasets.

Only 5 closed-source VLMs are tested (no open-source/other computer-use-specific models), limiting generality of the claims about 'current models' and reducing reproducibility since API-based proprietary models can change over time.

The 'file/bash operations' setting, which produces the best results, is itself a form of tool access very similar to the tool-based paradigm the paper argues against, which somewhat blurs the core contrast the paper is trying to draw between computer-use and tool-based agents.

Newly introduced task sets (IDE Configuration, General-SWE) lack detailed validation, human baseline performance, or inter-rater agreement information, making it hard to assess their quality/difficulty calibration.

Some qualitative claims (e.g., statistical significance on Intercode, or the symbolic renaming 0%→50% experiment) are based on very small sample sizes (e.g., 4 tasks), limiting the strength of the conclusions drawn from them.
The paper promises code/data release but the actual repository link is blank in the provided text, raising minor reproducibility concerns.
No variance/error bars are reported despite the inherent stochasticity acknowledged in the POMDP transition function, making it hard to judge robustness of the reported percentages.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated environment (PwP) combining computer-use agent evaluation with software engineering, a domain previously underexplored for CUAs and one with strong specialized baselines for comparison.

PwP-Bench aggregates 13 existing SWE datasets plus 2 new task sets into a unified, extensible benchmark spanning multiple languages, modalities, and task types (code generation, multimodal synthesis, domain-specific programming, general SWE tasks).

Extensive empirical evaluation across 9+ models and 3 agent designs (pure CUA, CUA+File/Bash API, specialized SWE agent), yielding a clear and interesting finding: pure visual CUAs underperform dramatically (22.9%) relative to text-API-augmented CUAs (50.7%) and specialized agents (48.8%).

Rich qualitative and quantitative failure analysis (visual grounding errors, inability to use advanced IDE tools, error recovery failures, tool-usage ablations) that provides actionable insight for future CUA development.

Good engineering effort: Docker-based sandboxed environment, gymnasium-style API, checkpointing support, DOM/Set-of-Marks support for visual grounding, and code/data release, supporting reproducibility and extensibility.

Thoughtful supplementary analyses (assisted-tool experiments, long-horizon 250-step evaluation, comparison tables against best reported specialized SWE agent scores) that strengthen the paper's central claims.
weaknesses: Main evaluations are run on PwP-Bench-Lite (300 instances, 20 per task) rather than the full 5400-instance benchmark, which limits statistical robustness of the reported percentages, especially for tasks with only 20 samples (e.g., SWE-Bench subsampled from 2000 instances) and could produce noisy comparisons; only one statistical significance test (McNemar's, for CTF) is reported anywhere in the paper.

Comparisons to 'best reported' specialized SWE agent scores (Appendix E.1) are not well-controlled: those numbers come from different evaluation subsets, inference-time scaling, fine-tuned models, and verifiers, making the comparison more illustrative than rigorous.

The step budget (20 steps, with a limited follow-up at 250 steps on only 3 datasets with 20 instances each) may be insufficient for complex SWE tasks like SWE-Bench, and the small-sample follow-up doesn't robustly establish whether the reported gap trends hold at realistic budgets.

The novel contribution of PwP-Bench itself is somewhat limited since 13/15 tasks are repurposed from existing datasets; the genuinely new content is 2 small task sets (VSCode config, General-SWE) with only 20 instances each, which is a small addition relative to the paper's framing.

Models evaluated (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5/3.7/4.0 Sonnet, Gemini-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL) are already becoming dated relative to more recent computer-use-specific models, which may limit the currency/generalizability of the conclusions, especially claims about rapid CUA improvement trends.

Macro-averaging across heterogeneous per-dataset metrics (accuracy vs. CLIP score vs. multi-metric averages) to produce a single 'Overall Avg' can obscure interpretability and comparability across very different task types.

Minor writing/proofreading issues (e.g., typos like 'Aas shown', 'potetntially', 'evluate', inconsistent table/figure numbering references) suggest the manuscript could benefit from another editing pass.

strengths: Addresses a timely and well-motivated question: whether generalist computer-use agents can match specialized software engineering agents, which is an interesting intersection of two active research areas.
The PwP environment is reasonably engineered infrastructure (Docker-based, VSCode-integrated, gymnasium-compatible, checkpointing support) that could be useful as a community resource if released.
The benchmark aggregates 13 existing datasets plus 2 new task sets across many languages and modalities, giving broad (if shallow) coverage.
Evaluation spans 9 different models across three agent designs (pure CUA, CUA+file/bash API, specialized SWE agent), offering a reasonably wide comparison.
Qualitative failure-mode analysis (visual grounding errors, inability to use debuggers/profilers, poor error recovery) is somewhat informative and illustrated with concrete examples.
Some additional ablations (assisted-tool experiment, 250-step evaluation, trajectory-level grounding error counts) attempt to probe the sources of the performance gap.
weaknesses: Core empirical results rely on PwP-Bench-Lite with only 20 instances per task (300 total across 15 highly heterogeneous tasks spanning 14 languages); this is a very thin sample for benchmark-level claims, and no variance/confidence intervals or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere in the main results, undermining the reliability of the headline numbers (e.g., many 0% cells for SWE-Bench-Multilingual, Bird, Minictx across almost all CUA settings).

The central finding -- that agents restricted to raw pixel-level actions underperform agents given direct file/bash text APIs -- is largely expected given prior literature on CUA grounding weaknesses (OSWorld, VisualWebArena) and does not constitute a particularly novel or surprising scientific insight; the paper mostly confirms known limitations in a new domain.

The comparison to 'best reported specialized SWE agent' scores in Appendix E is explicitly acknowledged as apples-to-oranges (different scaffolds, inference-time scaling, verifiers, and full dataset vs. the paper's 20-instance subset), yet is still used to support headline claims about CUAs 'approaching' specialist performance, which is methodologically weak.

Only one specialized baseline (mini-sweagent, with a single base model Claude-4.0) is used for direct controlled comparison; this is a narrow baseline set for claims about specialist vs. generalist agent performance across 15 diverse tasks.

Many per-task metrics are heterogeneous (different metrics per dataset, several averaged together), making the headline 'overall average' number somewhat opaque and hard to interpret or reproduce exactly.

The 'assisted agent' experiment, used to argue for future potential, is a hand-engineered, dataset-specific set of tool APIs for only 4 datasets -- this undercuts the paper's own thesis about task-agnostic generality and is more a tool-building exercise than evidence about CUA capability improvements.

No discussion of cost/efficiency trade-offs (token usage, wall-clock time, API cost) despite CUAs requiring many more steps/screenshots than specialized agents, which is an important practical dimension given the paper's claim of economic relevance.

The 20-step cap for most experiments is a significant constraint that likely penalizes CUAs disproportionately (confirmed by the paper's own 250-step ablation showing large gains on SWE-Bench), yet this ablation is only run on 3 of 15 tasks, leaving unclear how representative the main-table conclusions are for the rest of the benchmark.

Several qualitative claims (e.g., 'hallucination', 'misidentifying UI elements') are illustrated with single cherry-picked examples rather than systematic quantitative analysis across the whole benchmark, limiting the rigor of the failure-mode characterization.

The novelty of the technical approach is limited -- it largely combines existing techniques (Set-of-Marks, Anthropic's computer-use API design, existing SWE datasets) into a new environment rather than proposing new methods, which may be seen as primarily a benchmark/engineering contribution with correspondingly modest research novelty for a top-tier venue.

strengths: Introduces the first comprehensive computer-use environment (PwP) and benchmark (PwP-Bench) specifically targeting software engineering tasks, filling a clear gap between simple CUA benchmarks (web/OS) and specialized SWE agent evaluations.

Extensive evaluation across nine diverse models (open- and closed-weight, UI-trained and general VLMs) and three agent designs (pure CUA, CUA+File/Bash APIs, specialized SWE agent), providing a rich empirical picture.

Benchmark is genuinely broad: 15 tasks, 14 programming languages, multiple modalities (text, image, data files), and 5400 total instances unifying 13 existing datasets plus 2 novel task sets (IDE configuration, General-SWE) that probe underexplored IDE-tool-usage skills.

Strong, well-supported qualitative and quantitative analysis of failure modes: visual grounding error rates are explicitly quantified (e.g., 95% of GPT-4o trajectories contain grounding errors), with illustrative figures for each failure mode (misclicks, hallucinated state, wrong panel focus).

Thoughtful supplementary experiments strengthen the core claims: an 'assisted' tool-augmented setting quantifies headroom from better tool use, a targeted rename-refactoring probe shows prompting alone can triple accuracy, and a 250-step long-horizon ablation confirms trends are robust to the step-budget choice.

Good engineering contribution with reproducibility support: Dockerized sandboxed environment, gymnasium-style API, checkpointing for search/RL, and detailed comparison tables against prior environments/benchmarks and hand-engineered tool sets used by prior SWE agents.

Clear, well-organized writing with informative figures/tables that make the empirical narrative (pure CUA underperforms, APIs close much of the gap, agents rapidly improving over model generations) easy to follow.
weaknesses: Main evaluation relies on PwP-Bench-Lite with only ~20 instances per task (300 total out of 5400), which is a small sample for many sub-tasks and raises concerns about variance/statistical robustness of the reported per-task and category numbers.

Comparisons to 'best reported' specialized SWE agent scores (Appendix E) are not apples-to-apples: those numbers often come from different inference budgets, scaffolding, verifiers, and full dataset evaluation, while PwP's own numbers are from 20-sample subsets, making the headline comparisons only suggestive rather than rigorous.

Only one specialized SWE agent baseline (mini-sweagent, single Claude-4.0 backbone) is used for the central 'specialist vs. generalist' comparison; a more diverse set of specialized agents (e.g., Agentless, OpenHands, SWE-agent variants) would better support the paper's central claim.
Model coverage is inconsistent across settings (e.g., GUI-Owl-32B is evaluated only in the pure CUA setting but not with File/Bash APIs), weakening the completeness of cross-setting comparisons.

The 'CUA + File/Bash APIs' setting, which drives most of the paper's positive headline result, already deviates substantially from pure visual computer use, which somewhat blurs the central thesis about whether purely visual generalist agents can match specialists.

The paper is primarily an engineering/benchmark contribution rather than a methodological advance; no new agent architecture or training method is proposed to address the identified grounding/tool-use weaknesses, limiting technical novelty.
No human performance baseline is reported, which would help contextualize how large the remaining gap to a reasonable ceiling actually is.

Some analyses (e.g., visual grounding error quantification, error-recovery probing) are based on very small manually-annotated samples (20 trajectories, 5 scenarios), limiting the strength of the quantitative claims drawn from them.
